items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: I loved “Sing Along with Basie” because we were with Joe and the band.

ctx.x: Yeah, ’51 I think, if my notes are correct at all. And a vocalist in front of a big band, is it taxing?

I don’t like it. I feel too restricted. I’d much rather sing with a quartet, maybe piano, bass, drums and guitar or I love flutes and saxophones. There are some people who are brilliant at it. I don’t feel I’m one of those. Joe Williams was — I mean Sarah — any singer. But I felt looser when I was with a smaller group.
Tell me how the Farmer’s Market and that whole thing came about.

items.title: Annie Ross — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We had Joe Williams. Jon worked there, Blossom, Stuff Smith, and many, many, many people.

ctx.x: Yeah. We were sitting one day in my apartment, with friends. Somebody said, “Why don’t you open a club?” I said, “Well, number one, I’ve never had a club, and number two, we don’t have any money.” They said, “We do.” So Sean went to look for premises. He found space. It had been a Lyons tea shop. That’s a famous chain of tea places. Sean came back, and he said, “I’ve got it. It’s perfect. It’s downstairs. It’s across the street from the stage door of the Drury Lane Theatre.” They went with him, looked at the…

It had a bar. You went down these stairs. You went in the bar, which had a big glass front. So you could see the show that was going on. But if you wanted to sit in the room . . . I remember we were getting ready for the opening night. They were still hammering the stage together. We were totally booked out. Then word came that Judy Garland was going to arrive with about six people. Where to put six more people? But we did. We had a great staff.
